title.en: Uptake of minerals and the transport of food (phloem translocation)

heading.en: Sugar from leaves to a potato

hook.en: A potato tuber is mostly starch, yet it grows underground in the dark. Every gram of it was made in the leaves and carried down through the *phloem*.

title.en: Explain mineral uptake and its translocation

say.en: A potato tuber is mostly starch, yet it grows underground in the dark. Every gram of it was made in the leaves and carried down through the phloem. In this lesson: Explain mineral uptake and its translocation.
Describe source and sink.
Explain the pressure flow mass flow hypothesis.

body.en: *Minerals* are present in the soil as ions, often at lower concentration than in the root. Most enter root hair cells by active transport, using ATP; ion pumps in the endodermal membranes control which ions pass and how many. Once in the xylem they travel up with the transpiration stream to growing regions, leaves and fruits. Some, such as N, P, K and S, are later remobilised from old leaves to young parts through the phloem; Ca, which is part of cell walls, is not.

points.en: Xylem carries ions up; *phloem* remobilises some

body.en: Food (mainly sucrose) moves in the sieve tubes of the phloem from a source (a part that makes or releases sugar, like a mature leaf) to a sink (a part that uses or stores it, like roots, fruits or growing tips). At the source, sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes; water enters from the xylem by osmosis and turgor *pressure* rises. At the sink, sucrose is unloaded and water leaves, so the pressure falls. The sap flows en masse from high to low pressure: mass flow. Because sources and sinks can change, phloem flow can go up or down.

Sink: sugar unloaded, pressure low.
Flow is bidirectional; mainly sucrose.

narration.en: Sugar loading at the leaf draws in water and raises the pressure there. Unloading at the root lowers it. The difference drives the sap down the tube: faster loading, faster flow.

problem.en: In spring, before the leaves open, sugar maple sap rises from the roots. Use source and sink to explain this, and say why it does not contradict the pressure flow hypothesis.

steps.en: Starch stored in the roots is converted to sucrose; the roots are now the source.
The growing buds above are the sinks.
Loading at the root raises pressure there, so the sap flows up: the direction is set by where the source and sink are.

answer.en: The source is the root and the sink the buds; mass flow goes from source to sink

prompt.en: Put the steps of the pressure flow hypothesis in order.

steps.en: Sucrose is made in the mesophyll of the leaf (source).
Sucrose is actively loaded into the sieve tubes.
Water enters the sieve tubes from the xylem by osmosis.
Turgor pressure rises at the source end.
Sap moves by mass flow towards the sink.
Sucrose is unloaded at the sink and water leaves, lowering the pressure.
